name: Dana Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making the time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a troubleshooter for the electricity company in Millbrook, which means I'm usually on my own in a single-person bucket truck. When a power line goes down or a fuse blows, I'm the first one there. I work a rotation, a week of days and then a week of nights, and on nights I might get six calls or none.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of it. You pull up to a dark street, look at the poles, and work out where the fault is before the big crew shows up. The tough part is the nights in winter, and the drunk guy who comes out in his slippers to tell me how to do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, I didn't miss anything by not using it. I don't have any AI apps and I don't plan to. At work I'd shrug, because nothing on my truck would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing for me. I own my little house on Fenwick Street, I rent the spare room to Kayla, a nurse, and I've got nearly a year of money in savings. The work is steady and every town around here is short of troubleshooters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing exactly what I do. Day week, night week, pay the mortgage down a bit faster when there's storm overtime. Maybe redo the kitchen next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a regular Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI at all. Has anyone at work pushed you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new kid, Leo, keeps showing me how he asks his phone about fault codes. I tell him the pole will tell you more than the phone will. He thinks I'm a dinosaur, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the kitchen about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my reward to myself. I've been putting overtime aside for it since I bought the place. In this picture, I just go ahead and do it.

say: I'd say I **missed nothing** by never using AI.
At work I'd shrug, since nothing on my **truck** would change.
think: My job means **nothing new** for me in this picture.
I own my house, rent a room to Kayla and have nearly **a year saved**.
do: Keep the **day-week, night-week** rotation as it is.
Pay the **mortgage** down faster with storm overtime.
Redo the **kitchen** next year as a reward.
S0.quote: I tell the new kid Leo that the pole will tell you more than the phone will.
fieldNote: She's **proud** of not using AI and frames it as good judgement.
Her **house** and lodger income make her feel secure.
Her life plans are **small and steady**: a new kitchen, a faster mortgage.

steps.text: Keep the day-week, night-week troubleshooting rotation
Pay the mortgage down faster with storm overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good for the office, it doesn't touch my truck. Maybe they'd send me to the right pole faster, which I'd take. I'm not the type to post online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the part that would get me is dispatch. Right now Marlene in dispatch knows the town, she knows that a call from Ridge Road in a storm is probably the tree by the church. If an AI does dispatch, it might send me to the wrong end of town at three in the morning, and I'd be the one standing in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the same way, and I'd keep my own notebook of where the trouble spots are, like I do now. I'd put a bit more aside each month in case things get weird. I wouldn't sign up to test anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little annoyed thinking about the dispatch thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the AI dispatch turned out to be better than Marlene?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then fine, I'd use it, I'm not stupid. But I'd want to see it work through a whole winter first. Software that works in July doesn't mean much in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marlene, for sure, and the people at the call centre. They take the angry calls when the power's out. If a chatbot takes those, I think people get even angrier, and that lands on me when I show up.

say: I'd say it's good for the **office** and doesn't touch my **truck**.
I'd take faster routing to the right pole, but wouldn't post about it.
think: The worry is **AI dispatch** sending me to the wrong end of town at **3 a.m.**
Marlene in dispatch knows the town in a way **software** might not.
do: Keep my own **notebook** of trouble spots in town.
Put a bit **more aside** each month in case things get weird.
S1.quote: Software that works in July doesn't mean much in January.
fieldNote: Her concern is **practical**: wrong dispatch costs her time in the rain.
She'd accept AI if it **proved itself** through a full winter.
She worries about **angry customers** if chatbots take outage calls.

steps.text: Keep a notebook of Millbrook's trouble spots
Put more of each paycheck into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when a robot climbs Ridge Road in an ice storm. That's what I'd tell the guys at the yard, and probably my dad too. I'd keep quiet online, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be worried, but not panicking yet. The thinking part of my job, finding the fault, is exactly the kind of thing AI could do by 2028 from the smart meters. Then around 2031, when I'm thirty-two, a robot truck that can fix it shows up, and that's my whole job gone. I'd probably have a couple of years of the odd jobs after that, but I can see the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop the kitchen and throw that money at the mortgage. I'd rent out the second spare room too, so there's more coming in, and keep doing my job like normal while I see how real the robots are. If they still can't handle a downed line in the snow by 2030, I'd breathe easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd sleep fine for a year and then start lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see how real the robots are. Isn't that risky with only three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen big promises from the company before, like the self-healing grid that was supposed to end outages, and I still go out every night. I'm not jumping until I see the thing work in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad was a mechanic for thirty-five years and he'd say they said the same about computers in cars. I'd tell him it's different this time, I think, and he'd say prove it. We'd probably both be a bit right.

say: I'd tell the yard I'll believe it when a robot climbs **Ridge Road** in an **ice storm**.
I'd stay quiet online and talk mainly to the guys and my **dad**.
think: Finding faults from **smart meters** is thinking work AI could do by **2028**.
Robot trucks around **2031** would take the rest of my job by thirty-four.
do: Cancel the **kitchen** and put that money on the mortgage.
Rent out the **second spare room** for more income.
Wait until about **2030** to see if robots handle snowy downed lines.
feel: **Anxious**, sleeping fine for a year, then **lying awake**.
S2.quote: I'll believe it when a robot climbs Ridge Road in an ice storm.
fieldNote: She splits her job well: **fault finding** is thinking work, repair is hands-on.
Past **broken promises** from the company feed her wait-and-see stance.
Her savings and **house** let her stay anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Cancel the kitchen and put the money on the mortgage
Rent out the second spare room on Fenwick Street
Watch until 2030 whether robots handle snowy downed lines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, show me. But I'd say it a bit quieter, because five years is long enough that it's probably real. At the yard I'd ask the supervisor what the company's plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd start counting. AI does the fault finding by 2031, robots by 2034, I'm thirty-five. That's still eight good years of pay, and with the house nearly paid by then, I'd be in decent shape, but I'd need to do something else after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage every month so it's gone by 2033. I'd rent the second room and maybe the garage to Kayla's boyfriend for his motorbike. And I'd ask about moving to the underground cable fault team around 2032, because those faults are buried and hard to reach, so maybe the robots get there last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a list, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You avoid new technology. Would the underground team mean learning new kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, they use fault location gear, the thumper and the radar. I'd hate the first six months. But it's still a truck and a trench, not an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kitchen waits. It always waits, apparently. But the house being paid off matters more than a nice counter.

say: I'd still say **show me**, but quieter, since five years makes it **probably real**.
At the yard I'd ask the supervisor about the **company's plan**.
think: Robots by **2034** leave me about eight good years of **pay**.
With the **house nearly paid**, I'd be in decent shape but need something after.
do: Overpay the **mortgage** so it's gone by **2033**.
Rent the **second room** and the garage for extra income.
Ask to move to the **underground fault team** around 2032.
S3.quote: The house being paid off matters more than a nice counter.
fieldNote: She turns uncertainty into a **countdown** with clear dates.
She'd accept **new kit** only if it's still physical work, not an app.
Her plan rests on the **house** as a safety net.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage so it's cleared by 2033
Rent the second room and the garage for extra income
Apply to the underground cable fault team around 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and half of these predictions are wrong. At the yard I'd tell the young guys not to panic. I'd still be the dinosaur.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine for a long while. Robots by 2039, I'd be forty, with the house paid off. It's not great being out of work at forty, but I'd have time to see it coming and figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now for the first few years. Do the kitchen, pay the mortgage, keep my notebook. Maybe around year five I'd start thinking about the underground team or something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the back of my mind, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half these predictions are wrong. Which half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dates, usually. People said self-driving trucks would be everywhere five years ago, and I've seen one, once, on the highway. So ten years might be fifteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd tell your younger self starting the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I'd tell anybody, learn the trade properly. If robots do come, the people who really understand the grid will be the ones who check them.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and half these **predictions** are wrong.
I'd tell the young guys at the yard **not to panic**.
think: Robots by **2039** would find me forty with the house **paid off**.
Being out of work at **forty** isn't great, but I'd see it coming.
do: Do the **kitchen** and keep paying the mortgage.
Keep my **trouble-spot notebook** and work as normal.
Look at the **underground team** or other options around year five.
feel: **Uneasy**, in the back of my mind but not **keeping me up**.
S4.quote: If robots do come, the people who really understand the grid will be the ones who check them.
fieldNote: Her **scepticism** about dates is based on things she's seen, like self-driving trucks.
The decade lets her go back to **normal plans** like the kitchen.
Her advice is **old-fashioned**: learn the trade properly.

steps.text: Redo the kitchen and keep paying the mortgage
Revisit the underground team idea around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. Three years from the AI finding faults to a robot fixing them isn't enough time for someone like me who doesn't jump at new things. What would help is the company being straight with us about its plans, and a guarantee of a spot on the underground team or something like it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people want robots fixing their power at night. When I show up at two in the morning, the old folks are happy to see a person, and nobody's asked them.

headlineQuote: When I show up at two in the morning, the old folks are happy to see a person, and nobody's asked them.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** troubleshooter who works alone in a bucket truck in Millbrook.
She owns a **small house** with a lodger and nearly a year of savings.
She never uses AI and trusts her **own notebook** over any app.
She's calm in the mild pictures and **anxious** in the faster AGI ones.
Her plan is to **pay off the house**, add rent income and wait to see robots prove themselves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years from AI fault finding to **robot repair** is too short for her.
whatWouldHelp: **Straight talk** from the company and a guaranteed spot on the **underground team**.
